kind.post_text: :We use the word "potentially" because some of the films have conflicting estimates (represented by loss ranges), which means they might fall below the threshold (there are 17 loss-range films out of the 122 that might fall below the $100m threshold). A film like ''Black Adam'' isn't really one of the biggest money-losers of all-time if it only lost $50 million, but if it lost $100 million then it will be. Also, you need to bear in mind that unlike box-office grosses which are often exact and published by the distributors in many cases, these losses are highly speculative in any case. I think the word "potentially" helps to cement the fact that the list is not definitive. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 14:07, 19 January 2025 (UTC)

:You make good points, but whilst charts adjusted for inflation exist at country level (e.g. United States/United Kingdom) it is notoriously difficult to do at worldwide level where inflation varies from country to country. It is further complicated by the fact that some films (especially the Disney ones) have accumulated box-office across several releases, so it is virtually impossible to do unless you have a "seed" list like at [[List_of_highest-grossing_films#Highest-grossing_films_adjusted_for_inflation]]. :For some reason Box Office Mojo stopped updating the total while it was still playing in some territories. Even though it was 10 years ago I remember the incident well, because it caused us a massive problem at the time. We were watching it wracking up millions in Japan and German and yet the worldwide total just wasn't going up! We don't really know how much it ultimately grossed, but we do know it grossed more than what BOM have it down for, and we do know it grossed at least $1,290 million during its original (as opposed to $1,280 million) based on the individual tracked territories. It should be noted that The Numbers stopped tracking it even earlier than BOM, and has the gross at $1,271 million. Box Office Mojo also states that it grossed a further $24 million during a 2023 re-issue in Australia. This is not correct and is a symptom of the BOM [[WP:BOXOFFICE#Box_Office_Mojo|double-counting issue]]; ''Frozen'' grossed $22.5 million during its original release, and BOM has included the original gross in the reissue gross. Ergo, the re-release gross was actually more like $2 million, rather than $24 million. Based on my estimates, ''Frozen'' ultimately finished just a whisker off $1.3 billion. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 22:53, 26 January 2025 (UTC)

:The last paragraph lists several reasons why Hitler became vegetarian, including health reasons, psychological reasons, and ideological reasons. I have drawn this out more and switched the order of the sentence around. It is very difficult to avoid Nazi "propaganda" outright, because the best source for this information is Hitler himself and nearly all of the eyewitness testimony came from Nazis. Also, while you are welcome to add further content, please don't add new content and citations to the lead—that is what the article body is for. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 05:56, 27 January 2025 (UTC)

:::Mostly because it wasn't. Rynn Berry is not a credible authority on Hitler, and while Robert Payne actually met Hitler it was before the war. As explained in the article, all accounts of Hitler consuming meat pre-date his shift to vegetarianism. The last eyewitness account of Hitler consuming meat comes from 1937. Rynn Berry took these accounts out of context to prosecute his thesis that Hitler was never vegetarian. When his work was debunked, he conceded that Hitler may well have been vegetarian but not for "ethical reasons". That may or may not be true, but we will never know. Forensic analysis did not find any meat fibres in his teeth, and the woman who forced to become his food-taster in 1942 said that all of the food she was forced to test for Hitler was vegetarian. Hitler's vegetarianism did form part of Nazi propaganda, but for better or for worse all evidence points to the fact that he became vegetarian at the end of his life. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 06:47, 27 January 2025 (UTC)

:::The $1,306m figure is a result of double-counting Australia's original release gross. It made $22.5 million on its [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl1564641025/weekend/ original release] in Australia. BOM then counts this gross again in the [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl1685749761/weekend/ 2023 re-release], which is incorrect. So there are two problems going on here: i) BOM under-reported the original gross by around $10 million; ii) it then double-counted Australia's $22.5 million original release gross. Therefore it is over-shooting by about $12; if you deduct that figure from the worldwide total that would put the proper gross at around $1,294m give or take. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 20:24, 27 January 2025 (UTC)

:::::::The "gross" budget used to be in the infobox; it must have been removed at some point. The debate between whether the "gross" or "net" budget is the "true" budget is a debate that Wikipedia probably shouldn't enter IMO. Whilst the gross budget may be more representative of the value of the goods and services consumed during production, the "net" is more representative of the expenditure the studio ultimately accrues. The net budget is more in line with what is regularly reported in the trades like Deadline and Variety though, which is probably why there is a preference for it on Wikipedia. I am in favor of including both figures where they are available. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 11:59, 29 January 2025 (UTC)

That list puts the US gross at around $1.6 billion, but another estimate by ''Time'' [[The_Birth_of_a_Nation#Box_office|estimates it grossed $1.8 billion worldwide]]. Another estimate puts its admissions at [[Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)#Audience_response|around 50 million]] by 1930, an astonishing number when the population was much smaller, but by this time the sound era was taking off and the silents were falling out of fashion. By 1930, TBOAN had taken $10 million in global rentals, and a year later had a very successful re-release with sound effects which took its earnings to $15 million. After that its appeal started to dwindle. It is estimated that the film ultimately earned around $20 million, so it is possible that it generated 100 million admissions all-told, but the ''Inside Kino'' source has it an almost double. On what basis did they arrive at that conclusion? Given all of the estimate floating around I think we'd need further corroboration and some insight into the methodology before we go adding it to charts. kind.post_text: :It is next to impossible to pin down how much ''The Birth of a Nation'' has earned. The most reliable estimates put its gross rental at about $15–18 million ($35–45 million gross) around the time ''Gone with the Wind'' came out, but that is likely to be an under-estimate because it was sold on a "states rights" basis in the early years. ''Variety'' once estimated it had earned $50 million gross but later retracted the claim, and in fairness that's probably at the lower end. Some estimates run as high as $100 million gross (which is unlikely IMO, given how long it took ''Gone with the Wind'' to get there). The truth is that nobody knows how much it earned, and is unlikely to ever know. Richard Corliss estimated it had grossed $1.8 billion adjusted ten years ago, which would put it in the $2–2.5 billion range today, but that is based on some very subjective estimates. In some sense this is true of all films where the loss is estimated, because the marketing costs and the ancillary revenues are often the result of educated guesswork. It's just an unavoidable hazard of working on an article such as this. Personally I think films produced by publicly owned companies should publish a full set of accounts to offset tax evasion, but until the US treasury agrees with me then we just have to make the best of it. The way I think of this little project is that we are collating reputable published information about films losses; some of it may be accurate, some of it not, but it's all there for people to formulate their own judgments. I mean, if I see a loss estimate of $100 million based on a $180 million budget, and then it turns out the film cost twice that much, then obviously that throws the loss figure into serious doubt, but at least I have a baseline i.e. this film potentially lost 250 mil rather than 100 mil. == Scope of the article ==

In 2011 I created this article to provide an overview the corporate structure of the professional tour. The article remained in that form for over 13 years, until a couple of months ago when {{u|TheVictoriaHarbourer}} overhauled the article. == Excessive number of images added to the article ==

It appears a dispute that originated at another article has spilled over into this article. It seems that {{u|Clarityfiend}} challenged {{u|Ariadne000}} about overly long image captions at [[The Day the Earth Stood Still]]. The discussion can be viewed at [[User_talk:Ariadne000#Film_captions]]. Clarityfiend provided several examples of articles which exhibited good practice, this article being one of those. Ariadne000 subsequently [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)&oldid=1291487093 added a dozen photos with overly long captions]. I find Ariadne000's general approach to editing problematic, but I will just focus on the editorial problems:
# I agree with Clarityfiend's view that overly long captions usually reflect poor practice per [[MOS:CAPSUCCINCT]]. In my experience, overly long captions are usually symptomatic of problems with the article body, or maybe the image's lack of relevance to the sourced commentary of the article.
# Ariadne000 argues that "because GWTW is so iconic, photos are warranted". There is no policy or guideline based rationale for such justification. There needs to be an encyclopedic purpose for including an image per [[MOS:IMAGERELEVANCE]]: "''Each image in an article should have a clear and unique illustrative purpose and serve as an important illustrative aid to understanding''". While a couple of the photos have encyclopedic value, in that they would useful to illustrate sourced commentary, the general deployment here is primarily decorative. 
# Just because the images are available and free doesn't mean we have to use them. There has been no regard for the aesthetic of the value, or how it may look on somebody else's screen (see the screencap here: https://postimg.cc/JG1MVWSY). A lot of care was taken in the positioning of images and files throughout the article e.g. the music file was placed in the music section, the reissue poster in the "Later releases" section, the premier photo in the "Premiere" section and so on. By jamming this many photos into the article, the original photos and files are no longer correctly aligned with the relevant section. To maintain this alignment across different resolutions, images were limited to one per section.

Ariadne000 is displaying a [[WP:BATTLEGROUND]] mentality and in [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)&diff=prev&oldid=1291483046 their edit summary] referred to me as a "bogus" account that "doesn't get an opinion". I have been around well over decade and took this article through its GA review. Every editor is entitled to an opinion, but I am the editor best placed to explain the original design decisions. I would urge them to make their case here for the encyclopedic value of the images they wish to add, and if there is a consensus to add them then we can look at integrating them into the article rather than simply dumping them and destroying the aesthetic of the article. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 16:23, 21 May 2025 (UTC)

== Edits to the "Effects on children and BBFC classification" section ==

An anonymous editor has recently taken to restructuring the "Effects on children and BBFC classification" section in the article. The two section can be compared here:
# Original version: [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Watership_Down_(film)&oldid=1300479825#Effects_on_children_and_BBFC_classification]
# Re-structured version: [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Watership_Down_(film)&oldid=1300945994#BBFC_classification_revision_with_changing_attitudes_to_violence_in_children%E2%80%99s_films]

They take fundamentally different approaches. The original version introduces the controversy and then details the background over three subsequent paragraphs; namely: the BBFC, what initial critics thought, and recent criticism/scholarship. The new version approaches it in strictly chronologically fashion. I feel the first approach is more encyclopedic (and therefore more in keeping with Wikipedia) whereas the new version approaches it more as a news story with unfolding events.

I don't think the re-write is poor, but I do think it is inferior to the original version. I think the original version is far more succinct in summarizing the controversy, and then fleshing it out with background detail. I also find it mentally easier to parse (although I concede that may be because I am just more used to the original version). I would also like to add that I did not write the original version (so this is categorically not a case of me defending my own work). Generally, I don't think there are any policies/guidelines that would lead Wikipedia to prefer one over the other, so it is very much a personal preference thing. However, I would ask the anonymous editor to refrain from reverting and to respect [[WP:BRD]] until the issue is resolved. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 01:11, 18 July 2025 (UTC)

** As for the '''lead''' of the article, this is less formal and allows for a bit more discretion. It should list the stars of the film, but the lead can also identify other key members of the cast if the coverage in the article justifies mentioning them in the lead.

kind.post_text:
* '''Option 3''' – both dates with an accompanying note. Wikipedia has a preference for secondary sources over primary sources and the 1988 date dominates in that respect. A strict interpretation of [[WP:BLPPRIMARY]] and [[WP:WEIGHT]] would favor the 1988 date. However, there are numerous secondary sources that give an age that is consistent with 1987, rather than 1988, as per [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vanessa_Kirby&oldid=1310132902#cite_note-born-7 the note in the article]. The [https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/drama/who-is-vanessa-kirby-from-the-crown/ Radio Times] also gives 1987 as the year of her birth. It should also be noted that [https://www.imdb.com/name/nm3948952/ IMDB] goes with the 1987 date; while not a reliable source, IMDB is fairly accurate on the whole when it comes to birth dates. The most compelling evidence comes from primary sources, though:
** Public records for England and Wales show that there was no Vanessa Kirby born in 1988; and only one was [https://postimg.cc/gallery/gRD5Wzm born in 1987]. As you can see from the birth record the mother of the one born in 1987 has the same maiden name as the actress.
** The actress also has her own production company, [https://variety.com/2024/film/global/vanessa-kirby-aluna-labs-emerging-female-filmmakers-1236027204/ Aluna Entertainment]. The [https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/officers/nb0A4AKLrxOmZBmyJc2Tciz_Pf4/appointments government registration for this company] has Kirby's date of birth logged as April 1987. It should be noted that it is a criminal offence to provide false details to Companies House, and you also have to provide identification too.
:IMO, the primary sources (especially the government registration of her company} makes a compelling case for the 1987 date. While I appreciate that BLPPRIMARY establishes an important principle—it essentially exists to prevent editors creating "new" information that does not exist in secondary sources—I believe that strict observance in this case put Wikipedia in a position of propagating misinformation. The primary goal of Wikipedia is to disseminate facts. We do not actually need the primary sources to source the 1987 date so we would not actually be using primary sources to create new information, but just to reinforce the notion that there is factual discrepancy. We don't have to pick a side in these types of debates: presenting the case for both is a strength of Wikipedia. == In-universe revisionism == An editor has made several attempts to [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bruce_Wayne_%281989_film_series_character%29&diff=1311217956&oldid=1308609229 excise content] relevant to an encyclopedic understanding of the topic. The Joel Schumacher films were clearly intended to be sequels to the Tim Burton films at the time, and Warner has always [https://www.amazon.co.uk/Batman-Picture-Anthology-1989-1997-Blu-ray/dp/B001MUK7GY treated them as such]. They even share several characters played by the same actors, such as [[Pat Hingle]] (Commissioner Gordon) and [[Michael Gough]] (Alfred). Just because a later film retcons some of the earlier films out of canon does not alter the factual basis that the films were conceived and made at the time. From the perspective of ''Batman Forever'', Batman is the same character as that in the Burton films; from the perspective of ''The Flash'' maybe he isn't. This is not all that unusual; one example that springs to mind is [[Michael Myers (Halloween)]]: there are several different timelines for the character, but they are all manifestations of the same character from the original 1978 film. Outside of plot summaries, Wikipedia does not adopt an [[WP:INUNIVERSE]] perspective, and that needs to be respected here. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 05:31, 14 September 2025 (UTC)

== Dating of the events in the film ==

The article currently includes the following categories:
* [[:Category:Films set in 2002]]
* [[:Category:Films set in 2030]]

An editor also added a third: [[:Category:Films set in 2031]]. Whilst these dates may seem logical, editors should not be determining the dates themselves. Categories must adhere to [[WP:CATVER]] and [[WP:CATDEF]]. In this context CATVER means that the date must either be explicitly established by the film itself (in which case it should probably be included in the plot summary), or attributed to secondary reliable sources in the prose of the article. CATDEF means that the date should be a defining trait of the film itself; I think that is less of an issue here given that the temporal setting of the film is part of its premise. However, it is not clear why these exact dates are incorporated into the article. If the film does not explicitly establish the dates then less exact categories should be used i.e. [[:Category:Films set in the 2030s]]. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 18:05, 17 November 2025 (UTC)

kind.post_text: :I think "animal horror" can come under "[[natural horror]]" or "[[creature feature]]", and obviously there is significant overlap between the two sub-genres. However, I would say there are instances where "animal horror" would not be counted as natural horror (instances where the story is more sci-fi based, for example), but it is difficult to envisage a scenario where an animal horror would not be counted as a creature feature. "Plant horror" is probably more aligned with "natural horror", but I think there may be outliers where plant horror could be perceived as sci-fi horror rather than natural horror. One example that springs to mind is ''The Day of the Triffids'' where the plants are alien in origin; ironically that is included on this list, but I can easily envisage a counter-argument where one would not consider it natural horror on the basis that the natural world is not the origin of the horror. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 19:40, 18 November 2025 (UTC)

:Looking at that source, I would say it is not appropriate for this article. It does not utilise the term "natural horror", and it is clearly a list of films that just have a nature-based setting. This is apparent in its description of ''trollhunter'': "''While nature itself doesn’t play a villainous role in “Trollhunter,” the craggy mountains, majestic fjords and dense forests of Western Norway provide a stunning backdrop''." "Natural horror" is very specific in its conceptualisation: the horror has to emanate from the natural world. Thank you for drawing this source to our attention. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 20:35, 18 November 2025 (UTC)

:::I have never reviewed the source until now. It is part of the editorial process—subject to consensus—to determine which sources are appropriate. When the source qualifies some of its entries by saying "nature doesn't play a villainous role", I would say that explicitly goes against the general definition of the genre. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 21:50, 18 November 2025 (UTC)

:::::It uses the term loosely in reference to "previous lists". The source characterises the films on this list as "Our list for wilderness- and wildlife-centric horror films"—not quite the same thing as natural horror! It is even more explicit in the case of ''Trollhunter''—"nature itself doesn’t play a villainous role in “Trollhunter”. In "natural" horror the natural world is in some way the antagonist—not just used as a backkdrop—and by definition that excludes supernatural horror, where the horror emanates from beyond the natural world. If there other reputable sources that consider ''Trollhunter'' a natural horror we can revisit the question, but in this particular case we have a source of questionable RS status advancing a list of films under a much broader criteria than what is generally accepted. You can usually find a source for anything if you look hard enough, which is why we also have policies like [[WP:DUE]] and [[WP:BESTSOURCES]], and in your case [[WP:BURDEN]]. Just to take a handful of our regular sources: [https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/jaws Rotten Tomatoes] lists "Holiday, Mystery & Thriller, Horror, Adventure", [https://www.metacritic.com/movie/jaws/ Metacritic] & [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl3545925121/  Box Office Mojo] "Adventure, Horror, Thriller", [https://catalog.afi.com/Catalog/MovieDetailsPrintView/55193 AFI Catalog] lists the sub-genres as "Sea, Suspense" (which are essentially sub-types of adventure and thriller), and the [https://www.bbfc.co.uk/release/jaws-q29sbgvjdglvbjpwwc0yodqwmdm BBFC] goes with "Adventure, Thriller". kind.post_text: :The gross at BOM is incorrect. If you check the itemised grosses, you will see that BOM states it grossed $978 million on its initial release. This is incorrect: it is widely accepted that it grossed $913 million. Indeed, this is the figure BOM used to have: [https://web.archive.org/web/20200916195455/https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt0107290/]. The problem stems from a double-counting issue on BOM, where sometimes when a film is re-released the reissue gross is counted twice. There is a list of films afflicted by the problem here: [[WP:BOXOFFICEMOJO]]. You will note that ''Jurassic Park'' is one of the films listed, along with the correct gross of $1.038 billion, which is just below the cut-off, which is why it does not appear on the chart. We used to have a note explaining this, but I think it got deleted when it dropped off the chart. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 11:32, 23 December 2025 (UTC)

* '''Oppose''' – The title is already sufficiently disambiguated. The nomination regurgitates earlier nominations (such as those at [[Talk:Star Wars (film)/Archive 8#Requested move 6 June 2016]] and [[Talk:Star Wars (film)/Archive 10#Requested move (January 2023)]]) and addresses none of the counter-arguments that successfully resisted the rename. A summary of the counter-arguments:
:# Most people are familiar with the name change history, but it's not relevant. No evidence has been presented that ''Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope'' is the [[WP:COMMONNAME]] (which would render this whole debate moot if that were the case)—the official name does not take automatic precedence per the rationale at [[WP:OFFICIALNAME]].
:# The nomination also advances the false notion that "A New Hope" would serve as necessary disambiguation. This is not so: the article is already sufficiently disambiguated through the '''(film)''' disambiguation term, in accordance with [[WP:NCFILMDAB]]. No evidence has been presented that ''Star Wars (film)'' is being confused with the franchise. WP:NCFILMDAB does not preclude natural disambiguation, but it does not mandate a preference either way.
:# One argument that I do have some sympathy for is the consistency argument per the 5th criterion at [[WP:CRITERIA]] (the title is consistent with the pattern of similar articles' titles). However, this has to be balanced against the 4th criterion of concision (the title is not longer than necessary to identify the article's subject and distinguish it from other subjects). In any case, the natural disambiguation argument would only stack up if ''[[The Empire Strikes Back]]'' and ''[[Return of the Jedi]]'' were to also undergo similar name changes; however, these two titles do not require disambiguation, so they would be moved away from their more concise common names purely for consistency reasons, effectively over-riding the most important naming convention ([[WP:COMMONNAME]]). In truth, I am on the fence when considering this article in isolation, but when taken with the two immediate sequels I cannot get on board with it, which means the consistency argument breaks down.

The fact that the film does not appear on lists of cult movies alongside firmly established cult movies is a real red-herring for me. Neither is the film being proclaimed a "cult" movie by writers recognized as experts in film analysis. There is also a slight concern in that all of the sources are Indian; ordinarily this would not be an issue from a factual perspective, but there are language differences between different varieties of English (even American English and British English) and we need to be sure that when these terms are used they are applied consistently. On the subject of consistency, we should probably ignore what is written at the film article itself, logical fallacy or not. If an article does not cover a film's purported "cult" status then I think that weakens the case for adding the film to the list,  but total consistency across all the articles would depend on all editors applying the same standards and that is difficult to achieve. We need to be pragmatic about it. This dispute brings to mind another article I regularly work on: the [[List of box-office bombs]]. Many films have been described as bombs that didn't actually bomb—they just slightly under-performed; we are lucky because we have been able to apply a financial criteria for inclusion. Unfortunately, a film's cult status cannot be objectively measured, but you can still bring a similar level of rigour to a film's subjective consideration by applying the principle at [[WP:BESTSOURCES]], coupled with WP:CONTEXTMATTERS. Applying those principles, I am not convinced by the available sources that ''Raaz'' is a suitable inclusion on this list. == Over-linking of names ==

I accept there are instances where repeat linking is useful; for example, in sortable tables we cannot be sure in which order the names will occur. :It is not supported by the source. There is some justification that it may be true in the United States, but even then it is a stretch. There is no hard evidence because admissions are not tracked in most countries—only the box-office gross is tallied, and tickets cost different prices. ''Gone with the Wind'' had an extended roadshow for the first few months of its release where tickets cost more than double the typical price for the time. It also had another roadshow release in 1967, when it famously doubled its lifetime gross. ''Snow White'', on the other hand, went out at regular prices (and a large portion of its tickets were sold at concessionary rates for children), as did some other films, such as ''Titanic'' and ''Star Wars''. It is entirely plausible that one of these films sold more tickets than ''Gone with the Wind'' given how close they are to it on the adjusted charts. And that's before you get to China and India, where films generate huge admissions but do not threaten adjusted charts because of the much lower prices. It is not possible to state with any real conviction that one film has been watched more times in theaters than another. What we can say—and what is already stated in the article and backed up by credible sourcing—is that the film is the highest-grossing film of all-time in terms of adjusted box-office gross. :The update is almost certainly an issue with BOM: [[Wikipedia:WikiProject_Film/Film_finance_task_force#Box_Office_Mojo]]. The overseas gross was originally recorded as $450.6 million, and then at some point in 2024 it was randomly updated to $458.2 million. Whilst it is not impossible it could be a correction, an erroneous change to an initial gross figure in the case of films that have had re-releases is a long-standing issue with BOM. Sometimes the local distributor submits the full lifetime gross, which—depending on how they report it—leads to double-counting as part of the original gross or as part of the re-release gross. In the case of ''The Lion King'', this is almost certainly what happened, because [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/article/ed3093300228/ Disney itself issued a correction] to Box Office Mojo in 2016 where they clarified that ''The Lion King'' had indeed grossed $450.6 million overseas on its original release. Is it possible that Disney have corrected the gross yet again? It's not impossible, but there has been no reporting to that effect and given the known double-counting issue with BOM I would say it is strong odds the new figure is incorrect. * '''Comment''' Just to comment on the inconsistent approach of the BFI. I emailed them about this five years ago and, in short, it depends which ''department'' of the BFI is doing the classifying. The BFI Collections Database just uses the nationality of the production companies (which is why sometimes you will have several countries listed for a film); however, the Research and Statistic Unit attempts to take a more considered approach which takes into account a whole range of factors. Personally, I have found that the more discerning approach of the Research Unit tends to align better with the general perception of nationality identity (or "country of origin" as it is often known). The important thing to realize is that there is no universal approach and this is reflected in sources. The closest thing you will get to an "official" national identity is when a film is shot under an EU co-production treaty, but that doesn't really help us here. I believe that trying to determine the relative contributions of the various production companies is extremely challenging and probably comes under [[WP:OR]] anyway. The most relevant policy is [[WP:WEIGHT]] i.e. we should be looking to reflect how sources themselves categorise the film. This isn't straightforward either, given how few sources there are, and the inconsistency of the BFI on this matter (I would be much more willing to defer to the BFI if its two departments were aligned on the issue). The AFI Catalog has not logged it yet either, which further complicates the issue. However, I think it is rather telling that the Motion Pictures Producers of Japan (Eiren) do not consider it a Japanese move. == Box Office Mojo vs The Numbers ==

You will find that that BOM and The Numbers very rarely have the same figure for any film and, as such, which we have to make a decision about which figure to use. Obviously—this being a chart—you have to pick one. The BOM double-counting issue aside, we have found that BOM is generally better overall for accuracy than The Numbers, so there has been a long-standing tradition to default to BOM in the article—especially for the main chart—unless there is clear evidence that the figure is incorrect and another source offers a more accurate number. Sometimes the numbers fall out of sync because one source is updated before the other, but this in itself is not a good reason for defaulting to a different source, because Wikipedia is [[WP:NOTNEWS]]. kind.post_text: :If they still hold encyclopedic interest on that basis then that would need to be established by reliable sources in the future, on that basis, because the underlying conditions of their notability will have changed per [[WP:LISTN]]. It would probably require establishing a new list too, (e.g. ''List of films that entered the public domain through copyright registration errors'' or something to that effect), because you would need to provide an encyclopedic basis for why Wikipedia has created a list. I also don't agree that the list will "cease to exist"—copyright will continue to expire and notable films will continue to enter the public domain. Criteria will probably change over time as laws change i.e. the public domain is ever-expanding. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 08:14, 22 April 2026 (UTC)

kind.page: Talk:List of films in the public domain in the United States
kind.post_text: :::There are probably hundreds (if not thousands) of films that didn't renew their copyright terms—having a cut-off date is a sensible solution to prevent the list from becoming unwieldy. Changing the list to a list of films that did not max out their copyright terms potentially violates LISTN, but even more than that it would constitute a different type of list to what we have here. This article is literally about films currently in the public domain, and it handles this in the most efficient way. I'm not sure what benefit to readers adding hundreds of films would have, when we can just say that everything released before 1925 is in the PD. I also don't know how you draw the conclusion that the list will one day be empty: this is demonstrably not correct. Films will drop off as the cut-off date overtakes them, but more films will be added as their copyright terms expire. There is a bit of a gap at the moment because the need for registration was removed—along with extensions—but at some point in the future (2048 by my calculation) the list will start to grow again. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 05:19, 24 April 2026 (UTC)

* '''Comment''' I oppose re-framing the definition as ethical opposition to speciesism. Definitions of veganism do not generally invoke speciesism—they are generally grounded in rejecting the exploitation of animals; speciesism is concerned with animal exploitation too, but it's a philosophy that draws parallels between the agency of other species and that of people. This article covers the different aspects of veganism—ranging from ethical veganism to environmental veganism to religious or cultural veganism. We shouldn't be prioritising one particular form of veganism over another in the lead—this comes off as advocacy rather than encyclopedic commentary. The [https://www.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/definition/english/veganism dictionary] provides a basic definition based around eating and using animal products, and the [https://www.vegansociety.com/go-vegan/definition-veganism Vegan Society] fleshes this out a bit. The definition in the lead doesn't need to be any more complicated than that. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 04:07, 26 May 2026 (UTC)

:*:I don't think veganism necessarily precludes visiting a zoo, in the same it doesn't necessarily rule out buying a veggie burger from MacDonalds, although many vegans definitely rule those things out. As this [https://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/45274517 BBC article] says, a vegan  is "someone who doesn't eat or use animal products". The pure definition verifiably extends beyond just a diet, but the diet is generally the only thing that all vegans agree on. An environmental vegan is sometimes ok with buying second-hand leather products because it doesn't directly contribute to animal exploitation and contributes to sustainability, but an ethical vegan would not because an animal still died to create the product. Vegans often make exceptions for medication (which has often been tested on animals or may even use an animal derivative), which would actually be precluded from the pure definition. I work a lot on the [[List of vegans]], and the sources overwhelmingly only discuss diet, so it's not clear how "vegan" somebody is in other aspects of their life. So I think veganism extends beyond a diet, but there is not a strict consensus about what that entails. Usually, when someone is a dietary vegan and that choice carries over to no other aspect of their life (maybe it's a health kick or something) they are said to practice a plan-based diet. In practice, being a vegan generally involves not consuming animal derivatives as part of a diet and adopting a lifestyle that is less dependent on animal exploitation in other areas. In my experience, someone who does that would usually be regarded as a vegan or practicing veganism. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 16:21, 26 May 2026 (UTC)

This seems to offer little improvement over the actual Unicode 'half' character ('½') which is used in the wikilink anyway. If a user's system doesn't support ½, then it won't be able to open the link to that article – though I suppose in that edge case, you could argue that at least this article might display OK even if the link doesn't work. If Unicode is a stretch, how about an HTML entity? They've been a W3C recommendation since 1999, so unlikely to cause even the oldest of web-capable devices to break a sweat. That would make the film's title 8½ in the source, which is pretty human-readable if you can't have "8½". I wouldn't have noticed if 'frac' worked. But on my Mac (running Firefox on Mac OS 11 Big Sur) the text appeared initially as "8 1/2", then after I looked at the source and subsequently cancelled, it started appering as "8+1/2"! Looks like an issue with Template:Fraction, the Mediawiki codebase, or perhaps something else. == Article is venturing into WP:COATRACK territory ==

{{ping|Espngeek}} There are a number of problems with your edits to this article. First it is not a list, it is an article defining the themes and trends of blockbuster film-making. It is not necessary to add every single blockbuster you can dredge up, and it is arguably detrimental to the article. If readers want to see a list of blockbusters for a particular year they can visit the XXXX-in-year articles such as [[1982 in film]]. All that is necessary here is a few high-profile examples to flesh out the prose. Secondly, if I remove films on the basis that the claim about them is not corroborated by a source, then it is completely inappropriate to restore them without providing a source per [[WP:BURDEN]]. Some of your additions to this article seem highly selective and appear to reflect personal preference rather than objective, sourced, analysis. Something like [[Turner & Hooch]] for example was a reasonable hit grossing $70 million domestic (but far off the $100 million that was usually considered the "blockbuster" threshold of the 1980s) and only got middling reviews. That paragraph is specifically discussing "high-quality blockbuster". IMO it already lists far too many films, but those it should list need to meet this criteria and should be sourced to that effect. The bigger problem here is that you seem to be intent on turning this article into a list by the back door...it is NOT a list article, so please bear that in mind. == Addition of images to the article ==
An editor has repeatedly added multiple images to the article, per [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)&diff=prev&oldid=1384132145], [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)&diff=prev&oldid=1384132145] and [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)&diff=prev&oldid=1384211756]. I have repeatedly asked them to follow [[WP:BRD]] and initiate a discussion on the article talk page; I had hoped the editor would have adhered to thus guidance but apparently not, so I have taken the liberty of initiating the discussion instead.

;Inclusion
The editor's rationale appears to be that many articles about classic films have "loads of photos". This may be true, but this is a byproduct of the images themselves being in the public domain, not the product of a encyclopedic based rationale. The reasons the editor advanced on my talk page are
# illustrate the cast
# illustrate the production style
# give a graphic representation of the plot summary
# add visual interest to the article

These are not valid reasons in themselves. The relevant guideline for image inclusion is [[MOS:IMAGEREL]]. The pertinent bit states {{quote|''Images must be significant and relevant in the topic's context, not primarily decorative. Each image in an article should have a clear and unique illustrative purpose and serve as an important illustrative aid to understanding the subject ... However, not every article needs images, and too many can be distracting or cause undue weight: usually, less is more.''}}

* In this context the editors fourth reason is simply not valid per [[WP:NOTGALLERY]] (i.e. we don't add images to an article simply for the sake of adding images to the article). 
* The third reason is also a stretch: plot summaries do not need a "graphic representation". Wikipedia is not a comic-book. Plot summaries are descriptive by nature; indeed, both the American Film Catalog and IMDb get by without incorporating images of the plot. I cannot think of a single film article on Wikipedia where it has been necessary to add an image to the plot to help a reader further their understanding of the plot.
* The first reason is the most valid; however we don't "illustrate" the cast we "identify" the cast. It is worth bearing in mind that in this capacity a cast member usually only needs to be visually identified once, although if they further appear in "group" photos this is acceptable. The editor added an image of Leslie Howard and Olivia de Havilland to the cast section; I am actually open to this, as I agree that it would be a useful addition to the article, but there needs to be regard to the placement.
* The second reason is also valid to the extent that the production style needs to be illustrated i.e. whatever they are illustrating should be the subject of commentary. [[WP:NOTGALLERY]] clarifies this: "If you are interested in presenting a picture, please provide an encyclopedic context". In this context, I think the still of the Tara plantation meets the relevant criteria. The addition of the wedding costumes to the costumes section is primarily decorative. Yes, it's a costume, but it does not illustrate the concepts that are discussed. Furthermore, the section is too small to fully accommodate an image.

;Placement
The final point regards the concept of image placement, which the editor seems to have trouble with. The first couple of edits we just got an image dump. In the third we got a bit more effort, but it is worth bearing in mind what [[WP:GALLERY]] states: {{quote|''In articles that have several images, they are typically placed individually near the relevant text ... Generally, a gallery or cluster of images should not be added so long as there is space for images to be effectively presented adjacent to text.''}}

I have two points to make in this regard:
* The image should be in close proximity to the text that gives it encyclopedic value. If the image comes too early, the reader will not appreciate its significance; too late, and the reader has moved on. Ideally the text and the image should be in the same frame. Image dumps rarely achieve this because the images come first push the later images down, so they are no longer adjacent to the text. This defeats the purpose of adding the images in the first place. Given that displays are of different sizes, adding more than one image to a sub-section generally creates problems. If you intend to add more than one image, you should check how the article renders at ~1,000 pixels and at ~2,000 pixels wide, to ensure that the structure of the article remains robust. 
* When you add an image to a short-sub-section, or more than one image to a longer section the images can often protrude into the next section. Not only does this have ramifications for image placement in the next section, it is aesthetically poor and makes the article look amateurish. This is the primary problem with adding the image of Howard and de Havilland to the casting section—on wider displays it protrudes into the next section.

;Conclusion
So far, the editor's edits have been disruptive in that the addition of images has not been in accordance with the relevant style guidelines, and their manner has been combative rather than collegiate. I ask them to not add the images back into the article until the issues have been resolved and they have obtained a consensus for them. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 08:35, 8 November 2026 (UTC)

In the version on the left, the top row houses all of the psychological primary colors starting with yellow & blue, which are less common in color blindness (red/green blindness is more common). While editors are free to choose from any column, it makes sense to use the ordering of the colors to encourage colors that are less common in color blindness. You also have the anochromatic (white/black shades of gray) on the top row too; in reality, if you only need 2–3 colours it would actually be better to use the anochromatic spectrum. kind.post_text: ::::The other claims you cite are not unsourced, and they are different in nature. It is just a point of fact that Jaws is the prototypical summer blockbuster, and that aspect is covered in substantial detail throughout the article, and attributed to many sources. How "great" something is is a subjective opinion, not a fact. Firstly, a subjective opinion should not be offered in Wikipedia's voice, it should be attributed. Secondly, just because we can source a few lists of great films in which ''Jaws'' appears does not inherently make it one of the greatest films of all-time, in just the same way a bunch of positive reviews doesn't necessarily make a film well reviewed. We can say the claim has been made by this person or that list (which is what the article does) but we should refrain from drawing our own conclusions. Thirdly, proclaiming something the "greatest" (or one of) is an exceptional claim, which should require [[WP:EXCEPTIONAL]] sources, which simply do not exist in the article for this specific claim. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 16:00, 15 July 2026 (UTC)

items.post_text:
== Box Office Mojo vs The Numbers ==

You will find that that BOM and The Numbers very rarely have the same figure for any film and, as such, which we have to make a decision about which figure to use. Obviously—this being a chart—you have to pick one. The BOM double-counting issue aside, we have found that BOM is generally better overall for accuracy than The Numbers, so there has been a long-standing tradition to default to BOM in the article—especially for the main chart—unless there is clear evidence that the figure is incorrect and another source offers a more accurate number. Sometimes the numbers fall out of sync because one source is updated before the other, but this in itself is not a good reason for defaulting to a different source, because Wikipedia is [[WP:NOTNEWS]]. If we know the source will be updated in the near future we can stick with the current source and wait for it to be updated. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 22:46, 17 February 2026 (UTC)
items.discussion_title: Box Office Mojo vs The Numbers

items.post_text: :They employ different methodologies., so are representing different types of losses. This article assesses overall loss (including projected ancillary revenue). This is what [https://deadline.com/2025/03/snow-white-bombs-rachel-zegler-1236354912/ Deadline] states: {{quote|Disney‘s Rachel Zegler– and Gal Gadot-starring Snow White is headed to an estimated loss of $115 million after all global home entertainment, TV and Disney+ ancillaries, according to distribution sources Monday. The loss, which was expected, is based on a final worldwide box office of $225M.}} [https://www.forbes.com/sites/carolinereid/2026/02/10/disney-loses-170-million-on-snow-white-as-studio-reveals-movie-blew-its-budget/ Forbes] makes it clear the $170 million loss is based only on the box-office take: {{quote|The share of the box office isn’t the studio’s only return from a movie so offsetting it from the costs in the financial statements does not show whether it made a profit or a loss overall. As a Disney spokesperson told me in 2023, "there will be other income generated by the production (such as DVD/Blu Ray sales, merchandising, etc.). It’s not reflecting a true account of whether the film was overall profitable."}} So the two publications are using different methodologies to assess the level of failure. The Deadline approach is the one that is more consistent with the other entries on the list; it's true it's an early estimate, but Deadline will probably review the calculation when it does its round-up of 2025 flops, and The Numbers may revise that further. While Forbes is the most accurate source for budgets (because it accesses audited accounts through HMRC) its loss calculations are just estimates, that ignore several important factors. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 00:54, 2 March 2026 (UTC)

:The gross at BOM is incorrect. If you check the itemised grosses, you will see that BOM states it grossed $978 million on its initial release. This is incorrect: it is widely accepted that it grossed $913 million. Indeed, this is the figure BOM used to have: [https://web.archive.org/web/20200916195455/https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt0107290/]. The problem stems from a double-counting issue on BOM, where sometimes when a film is re-released the reissue gross is counted twice. There is a list of films afflicted by the problem here: [[WP:BOXOFFICEMOJO]]. You will note that ''Jurassic Park'' is one of the films listed, along with the correct gross of $1.038 billion, which is just below the cut-off, which is why it does not appear on the chart. We used to have a note explaining this, but I think it got deleted when it dropped off the chart. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 11:32, 23 December 2025 (UTC)

items.post_text: :::These are low-quality sources and their methodology is flawed. They have simply deducted the box-office gross from the costs, with no accounting for theater cut or ancillary sales. The only high-quality source in there is Variety which not provide a loss figure, and actually states that 60% of the budget for ''Borderlands'' was recouped through "pre-sales". If ''Variety'' is correct in its analysis then ''Borderlands'' is probably looking at losses of around $50 million. Please stick to reliable industry sources. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 12:26, 5 February 2025 (UTC)

items.post_text: :The article states "the studio is said to have lost around $114 million on the film", but is careful to not attribute to the CEO. If that loss estimate came from the CEO why not quote him, or attribute it to him? Geektyrant actually gets the info from [https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/business-news/lionsgate-quarterly-loss-1236055955/ The Hollywood Reporter] (a high-quality source) which has an in-depth interview with the CEO of Lionsgate in which the film's performance is described simply as "poor". Neither he, nor the article, provides a figure. This is why it is important to stick to [[WP:BESTSOURCES]]. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 02:24, 23 February 2025 (UTC)

items.post_text: :The update is almost certainly an issue with BOM: [[Wikipedia:WikiProject_Film/Film_finance_task_force#Box_Office_Mojo]]. The overseas gross was originally recorded as $450.6 million, and then at some point in 2024 it was randomly updated to $458.2 million. Whilst it is not impossible it could be a correction, an erroneous change to an initial gross figure in the case of films that have had re-releases is a long-standing issue with BOM. Sometimes the local distributor submits the full lifetime gross, which—depending on how they report it—leads to double-counting as part of the original gross or as part of the re-release gross. In the case of ''The Lion King'', this is almost certainly what happened, because [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/article/ed3093300228/ Disney itself issued a correction] to Box Office Mojo in 2016 where they clarified that ''The Lion King'' had indeed grossed $450.6 million overseas on its original release. Is it possible that Disney have corrected the gross yet again? It's not impossible, but there has been no reporting to that effect and given the known double-counting issue with BOM I would say it is strong odds the new figure is incorrect. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 00:43, 30 January 2026 (UTC)

::::::::Using Box Office Mojo or articles that cite BOM is completely fine, if they are reliable sources. We would only not use them when we have demonstrable evidence they are wrong. The grosses of Chinese films are much more difficult to track, due to patchier coverage. In this case, BOM and The Numbers stopped tracking the non-Chinese grosses quite a while ago. The Caixin source is China based and it is a reliable source for the $60 million figure, unless there is evidence to suggest it is wrong. Reliable sources do not have to provide their working out; we only second-guess them if they contradict themselves or they are contradicted by other sources. If you can provide evidence of an error we will take a look at that, we have a good track record when it comes to weeding out errors. But what we can't do is start disseminating numbers that are different to elsewhere unless we can clearly explain why the reported figure is wrong. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 21:49, 29 May 2025 (UTC)
items.discussion_title: Ne Zha 2's citations do not support its inaccurate figure

items.post_text: :We use the word "potentially" because some of the films have conflicting estimates (represented by loss ranges), which means they might fall below the threshold (there are 17 loss-range films out of the 122 that might fall below the $100m threshold). A film like ''Black Adam'' isn't really one of the biggest money-losers of all-time if it only lost $50 million, but if it lost $100 million then it will be. Also, you need to bear in mind that unlike box-office grosses which are often exact and published by the distributors in many cases, these losses are highly speculative in any case. I think the word "potentially" helps to cement the fact that the list is not definitive. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 14:07, 19 January 2025 (UTC)

:For some reason Box Office Mojo stopped updating the total while it was still playing in some territories. Even though it was 10 years ago I remember the incident well, because it caused us a massive problem at the time. We were watching it wracking up millions in Japan and German and yet the worldwide total just wasn't going up! We don't really know how much it ultimately grossed, but we do know it grossed more than what BOM have it down for, and we do know it grossed at least $1,290 million during its original (as opposed to $1,280 million) based on the individual tracked territories. It should be noted that The Numbers stopped tracking it even earlier than BOM, and has the gross at $1,271 million. Box Office Mojo also states that it grossed a further $24 million during a 2023 re-issue in Australia. This is not correct and is a symptom of the BOM [[WP:BOXOFFICE#Box_Office_Mojo|double-counting issue]]; ''Frozen'' grossed $22.5 million during its original release, and BOM has included the original gross in the reissue gross. Ergo, the re-release gross was actually more like $2 million, rather than $24 million. Based on my estimates, ''Frozen'' ultimately finished just a whisker off $1.3 billion. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 22:53, 26 January 2025 (UTC)

:::The $1,306m figure is a result of double-counting Australia's original release gross. It made $22.5 million on its [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl1564641025/weekend/ original release] in Australia. BOM then counts this gross again in the [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl1685749761/weekend/ 2023 re-release], which is incorrect. So there are two problems going on here: i) BOM under-reported the original gross by around $10 million; ii) it then double-counted Australia's $22.5 million original release gross. Therefore it is over-shooting by about $12; if you deduct that figure from the worldwide total that would put the proper gross at around $1,294m give or take. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 20:24, 27 January 2025 (UTC)

:::::::The "gross" budget used to be in the infobox; it must have been removed at some point. The debate between whether the "gross" or "net" budget is the "true" budget is a debate that Wikipedia probably shouldn't enter IMO. Whilst the gross budget may be more representative of the value of the goods and services consumed during production, the "net" is more representative of the expenditure the studio ultimately accrues. The net budget is more in line with what is regularly reported in the trades like Deadline and Variety though, which is probably why there is a preference for it on Wikipedia. I am in favor of including both figures where they are available. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 11:59, 29 January 2025 (UTC)

:You make good points, but whilst charts adjusted for inflation exist at country level (e.g. United States/United Kingdom) it is notoriously difficult to do at worldwide level where inflation varies from country to country. It is further complicated by the fact that some films (especially the Disney ones) have accumulated box-office across several releases, so it is virtually impossible to do unless you have a "seed" list like at [[List_of_highest-grossing_films#Highest-grossing_films_adjusted_for_inflation]]. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 02:37, 21 January 2025 (UTC)

items.post_text: :::::Pre-sales don't apply to anything after it came out. It is fixed income that was received prior to release. If it's lost $100 million+ then the industry trades will report it. items.post_text: :Actually, if you check the drop down on the BBFC it says that the original release is 243 minutes, and that the 2013 release is 251 minutes. The later version will be the restored version. The BBFC is the best source for time because in the days of film they would physically measure the length of the film (as opposed to just timing it), so it's the gold standard. There is no conflict here so I have corrected the time in the infobox. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 19:01, 7 February 2025 (UTC)

:I tend to always leave the inflation adjustment until about halfway through the year because the price index is unstable throughout the first quarter. It's not like there is a new film waiting to enter the chart so there's no hurry to update it. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 19:06, 8 February 2025 (UTC)

:My suggestion is to just stick with the Entgroup source for now and keep archiving it at Wayback. If it starts going down as a result of conversion rates then we can use the archived source. It's a difficult situation to deal with, and we'll just have to manage it the best we can in lieu of a better source. The bigger problem for us right now is [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt15242330/ this], which BOM claims $1.073 billion. I am assuming this is a mistake? Unfortunately basic competence at Box Office Mojo appears to be too much to ask for these days. I can understand the gross for some obscure film being wrong, but you'd think they could at least put some effort into keeping the top 200 chart accurate... [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 19:02, 9 February 2025 (UTC)

items.post_text: :Its racism isn't really a factor for a list like this. ''Gone with the wind'' glamorizes slavery and we include that. As far as I'm aware nobody really knows how much TBOAN grossed, or indeed how many people saw it because of inaccurate record-keeping and the fact it was sold on a "states rights" basis. That list puts the US gross at around $1.6 billion, but another estimate by ''Time'' [[The_Birth_of_a_Nation#Box_office|estimates it grossed $1.8 billion worldwide]]. Another estimate puts its admissions at [[Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)#Audience_response|around 50 million]] by 1930, an astonishing number when the population was much smaller, but by this time the sound era was taking off and the silents were falling out of fashion. By 1930, TBOAN had taken $10 million in global rentals, and a year later had a very successful re-release with sound effects which took its earnings to $15 million. After that its appeal started to dwindle. It is estimated that the film ultimately earned around $20 million, so it is possible that it generated 100 million admissions all-told, but the ''Inside Kino'' source has it an almost double. On what basis did they arrive at that conclusion? Given all of the estimate floating around I think we'd need further corroboration and some insight into the methodology before we go adding it to charts. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 20:23, 15 February 2025 (UTC)

items.post_text: :The new lifetime total at Box Office Mojo is incorrect. The re-release gross for for 2024 double-counts the original Australian gross. As you can see at the entry for the 2024 reissue, ''The Dark Knight Rises'' opened with $44,000 dollars, and the total went up to $29.6 million: [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/releasegroup/gr1701008133/]. Incidentally, if you add $29.6 million on to the original gross of $1.085 billion, then you get the figure of $1.115 billion. This higher figure is plain wrong, because the Australian re-release gross is double counting the gross from the original Australian release. If you had bother to follow the link I had provided in my edit summary (rather than edit-warring) then all of this clearly explained at [[WP:BOXOFFICEMOJO]]. The outline of the issue even provides a link to the discussion with representatives of Box Office Mojo: https://web.archive.org/web/20201111022424/https://community-imdb.sprinklr.com/conversations/imdbcom/tons-of-data-corruption-at-box-office-mojo/5f4a7cb68815453dba106d8f. Pay particular attention to Murray's answer: {{quote|The cause of these problems is that distributors are inconsistent when reporting data for re-releases; sometimes they start counting gross-to-date from zero, and sometimes they start reporting it from the last known value, even if it was decades ago.}} [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 05:02, 26 March 2025 (UTC)

:It is next to impossible to pin down how much ''The Birth of a Nation'' has earned. The most reliable estimates put its gross rental at about $15–18 million ($35–45 million gross) around the time ''Gone with the Wind'' came out, but that is likely to be an under-estimate because it was sold on a "states rights" basis in the early years. ''Variety'' once estimated it had earned $50 million gross but later retracted the claim, and in fairness that's probably at the lower end. Some estimates run as high as $100 million gross (which is unlikely IMO, given how long it took ''Gone with the Wind'' to get there). The truth is that nobody knows how much it earned, and is unlikely to ever know. Richard Corliss estimated it had grossed $1.8 billion adjusted ten years ago, which would put it in the $2–2.5 billion range today, but that is based on some very subjective estimates. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 00:46, 4 April 2025 (UTC)

items.post_text: :Obviously when the losses are based on an estimate of how much a film cost then a wildly inaccurate budget will increase the margin of error. In some sense this is true of all films where the loss is estimated, because the marketing costs and the ancillary revenues are often the result of educated guesswork. It's just an unavoidable hazard of working on an article such as this. Personally I think films produced by publicly owned companies should publish a full set of accounts to offset tax evasion, but until the US treasury agrees with me then we just have to make the best of it. The way I think of this little project is that we are collating reputable published information about films losses; some of it may be accurate, some of it not, but it's all there for people to formulate their own judgments. I mean, if I see a loss estimate of $100 million based on a $180 million budget, and then it turns out the film cost twice that much, then obviously that throws the loss figure into serious doubt, but at least I have a baseline i.e. this film potentially lost 250 mil rather than 100 mil. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 21:52, 6 April 2025 (UTC)

items.post_text:
==Jurassic World: Dominion ==

An editor has repeatedly [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_most_expensive_films&diff=prev&oldid=1289166930 updated the figures] for [[Jurassic World: Dominion]] using [https://www.theguardian.com/film/2025/apr/20/uk-taxpayers-contributed-89m-to-the-most-expensive-movie-ever-made this source]. The problem, though, is that the source does not corroborate the figure. The article states "the net cost of making Dominion [is] £361.7m". I don't take issue with the source's RS status but the figures are in sterling and do not provide a dollar conversion. Based on currency fluctuations it is likely the eventual budget was over $400 million, but it is not obvious to the reader how one arrives at the precise figure of $465 million. If you are going to add new figures to the article it needs to be clear where they come from. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 22:58, 6 May 2025 (UTC)

::I have just trimmed the trimmed list. The only reason we maintain it is in case we need a few extra films when we change the threshold, or in case some of the films in the article list are revised downwards. Nothing below 80 mil is re-entering the main list, and it is doubtful anything below 90 mil is. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 18:18, 7 May 2025 (UTC)

:We won't ever be taking the threshold down to $70 million, the threshold will go up every year. We are looking at $110 million next year, or maybe even $120 million depending on how many flops we get this year. Ultimately, we are documenting the biggest bombs of all-time with this list, and films that lose $70 mil are just not top-tier flops these days. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 18:41, 7 May 2025 (UTC)

* '''Comment''' I don't quite understand what the issue is. ''The Hollywood Reporter'' is not speculating, they are reporting what they have been told just in the same way as other publications. They clearly attribute their figure for the budget to their own sources. This is precisely the kind of situation the infobox guidance was created for, to prevent cherry-picking. The only scenario in which we would disregard alternative figures is if an officially audited figured is released down the line, as sometimes happens with the Disney budgets. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 05:07, 10 June 2025 (UTC)

*::All secondary sources repeat somebody else's number. That is how they work. How else would they obtain the information? It is Adulitanum that is referring to the figure as "speculation", not THR. THR states the budget "climbed to $100 million, according to sources". [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 05:35, 10 June 2025 (UTC)

:There is also [[WP:AGEMATTERS]] to take into account. It is often the case that a budget will increase during production. If sources are providing alternatives figures for the final cost that is something the article needs to recognize, but if there is a consensus among the sources that the film cost more than the budget that was greenlit I don't think we should be incorporating dated information into the infobox. IT's not really what we mean by cherry-picking because we have a clear rationale for excluding the older figure. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 21:29, 12 June 2025 (UTC)

:::That is not my interpretation of the guidelines. The phrase "...This is the cost of the actual filming" seems fairly unequivocal; I have never seen a case for the greenlit budget being added to the infobox, if different from the final cost. What the film cost to make is ultimately what is relevant to most readers. The meaning of "do not cherry-pick" is clear to me: do not apply your own subjective criteria based on a personal preference for a particular source. If there are clear objective reasons—such as audited figure becoming available, or an older figure that has been superseded by a newer estimate—then that is not cherry-picking. The Hollywood Reporter couches its estimate in clear terms: the film was ''initially greenlit'' at $80 million, and a [https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/ryan-coogler-sinners-box-office-opening-1236193272/ week later] reported the $90 million figure that is being reported elsewhere. I have no problem with including the information in those same terms, but it is fairly evident THR is no longer behind the claim that the film cost $80 million to make. If there are other reputable sources still making a case for the 80 mil figure then fair enough, but it seems pretty clear to me THR is no longer standing by it. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 17:44, 15 June 2025 (UTC)

::All of the box-office data generally comes from Box Office Mojo unless otherwise stated. If it isn't itemized collectively, then it is taken from the individual entries. Unfortunately, Box Office Mojo and The Numbers are inconsistent when it comes to including spin-offs. As Luke points out, The Numbers lists ''Catwoman'' and ''The Joker'' films under the ''Batman'' entry (and includes ''Supergirl'' under the ''Superman'' entry), but for no discernible reason omits ''Venom'' from the ''Spider-Man'' entry. There are many other examples where the trackers contradict each other and do not apply a consistent inclusion criteria. There is no demonstrable difference in the relationship between ''Joker'' and ''Venom'', and their parent franchises. It does leave us with the problem of how to compile the information, though. You can either mimic the trackers and accept the inconsistencies, or you can apply a consistent inclusion criteria. It is easy enough to verify that ''Venom'' belongs the ''Spider-Man'' franchise, via reputable sources such as [https://time.com/7098770/venom-the-last-dance-sony-spider-man/ this], and then we just take advantage of the leeway afforded by [[WP:CALC]]. I wouldn't describe Wikipedia as "doing it differently", it is just filling the gaps with sourced information where the trackers have been inconsistent. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 12:15, 29 June 2025 (UTC)

:::::Wikipedia articles are prohibited from making claims based on other Wikipedia articles per [[WP:CIRCULAR]]. If a claim cannot be sourced independently then it does not belong in the article. The ''Time'' article does not advance the argument that the SSU films are a separate ''franchise''—it simply acknowledges there is a wider body of work in the franchise beyond the core films just featuring Spider-Man. The Spider-Man franchise houses all the characters that exist under the Spider-Man copyright; when Sony licensed the rights to the Spider-Man IP they got the use of all of the other Spider-Man characters too: [https://web.archive.org/web/20231213011250/https://www.gq.com/story/sonys-weird-spider-man-extended-universe-explained-to-the-extent-that-its-explicable]. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 14:09, 29 June 2025 (UTC)

:::::::What the ''Time'' article is saying is that there are two types of movie in the franchise: the Spider-Man movies, and those known as the "Sony’s Spider-Man Universe". They are all on the same license ergo legally the same franchise. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 14:44, 29 June 2025 (UTC)

::Yeah, The Numbers is not taking a consistent approach to how it handles team-ups. You can't add ''Justice League'' to Superman and keep the ''Avengers'' movies out of ''Iron Man''—it would not be logical or defendable. The whole point of having a ranked chart is that each entry is subject to the same inclusion criteria. An alternative approach would be to just include every film a character has appeared in under their entry but then you lose the IP-centric approach of the list. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 23:55, 24 July 2025 (UTC)

:It's a good question, and there is a precise answer: ''King Kong'', while successful, was not a box-office smash upon original release. Much of its rental gross ($5.3 million) came from successful re-releases in 1938, 1944 and 1952, and the year charts only cover the original release. Variety's early rentals charts only cover domestic business too, and ''King Kong's'' original gross had an unusually high foreign share: of its $1,856,000 worldwide gross, only $745,000 came from the domestic box-office, which wouldn't see it make the top 10. Hope that answers your question. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 06:48, 5 September 2025 (UTC)

items.post_text: :I'm sure it would be technically possible, but the problem for me is that I don't particularly relish the prospect of the inevitable conflict that would result from rolling out corrections to dozens of articles. As you will be aware of, many articles have their own dedicated "guardians" which can be pretty resistant to external changes being imposed. You are potentially looking at a protracted discussion, followed by a heated RFC, and multiply that across dozens of articles. One of the reasons I prefer working on list-class articles is that we can pool the correct information on a single page and maintain it in one place. My hope is that awareness of the issue increases and the problem will become self-correcting. BOM are aware of the issue and correct the grosses over time, but it is disappointing that after 5 years (I think!) of it occurring they still have not found a permanent fix. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 01:11, 24 December 2025 (UTC)
items.discussion_title: Why is Jurassic Park (1993) not in the list?

items.post_text: ::Reading the Wikipedia article (especially [[Aztec Batman: Clash of Empires#Music]]) it appears to utilise ''Batman'' IP and is co-produced by DC, so it appears to be a legitimate spin-off. BOM only tends to list films under the franchise entries if they have had a domestic release, so that may explain its omission. ::::Yeah, it was limited to 10. The limit has served us well for 14 years! I have increased it to [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Template:Highest-grossing_films_franchise/franchise&diff=prev&oldid=1329842254 12]. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 06:15, 28 December 2025 (UTC)

:::If people want a list of $1 billion grossers they can get that information from Box Office Mojo; the purpose of this article is not to provide a ranked chart but to cover a topic, and we do that from several different perspectives. :It is not supported by the source. There is some justification that it may be true in the United States, but even then it is a stretch. There is no hard evidence because admissions are not tracked in most countries—only the box-office gross is tallied, and tickets cost different prices. ''Gone with the Wind'' had an extended roadshow for the first few months of its release where tickets cost more than double the typical price for the time. It also had another roadshow release in 1967, when it famously doubled its lifetime gross. ''Snow White'', on the other hand, went out at regular prices (and a large portion of its tickets were sold at concessionary rates for children), as did some other films, such as ''Titanic'' and ''Star Wars''. It is entirely plausible that one of these films sold more tickets than ''Gone with the Wind'' given how close they are to it on the adjusted charts. And that's before you get to China and India, where films generate huge admissions but do not threaten adjusted charts because of the much lower prices. It is not possible to state with any real conviction that one film has been watched more times in theaters than another. What we can say—and what is already stated in the article and backed up by credible sourcing—is that the film is the highest-grossing film of all-time in terms of adjusted box-office gross. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 09:57, 19 January 2026 (UTC)

''The Wizard of Oz'' is considered the film "seen by more viewers than any other movie" by the [https://www.loc.gov/exhibits/oz/ozsect2.html U.S. Library of Congress], but again it is highly subjective because there is no data that effect. The only data that is collected is box-office grosses, video sales and television viewings. There is no way rational way of deriving how many people have seen whatever film. Even if you limit the criteria to theaters (which the source does not do, btw) we don't know how many people have seen the film in the theaters. We only know the box-office gross. What we can say with some conviction is that it is the highest-grossing film ever (adjusted for inflation); that is borne out by clear numerical evidence.
