So the problem is not the source, the problem is the conversion figure. You cannot use a 2026 exchange rate for a film that did its business in 2025. Let's just use the higher Chinese gross as an example:
::* 15,462,577,300 / 6.9088 (current rate) = $2.238 billion
::* 15,462,577,300 / 7.1726 (June 2025 rate) = $2.156 billion
::If you check the exchange rate at https://www.xe.com/currencycharts/?from=USD&to=CNY&view=1Y during the first half of 2025 (when Ne Zha 2 made most of its money), the exchange rate peaked at CN¥ 7.3359 : 1 USD, and never went below CN¥ 7.1706 : 1 USD. So what do those convert to:
::* 15,462,577,300 / 7.1706 (low Jan–June 2025 rate) = $2.156 billion
::* 15,462,577,300 / 7.3359 (high Jan–June 2025 rate) = $2.108 billion
::So during the time it grossed most of its money, the Chinese gross CN¥ 15,462,577,300 can only convert to a dollar amount between $2.108–2.156 billion, and Entgroup (the sourced used by the article) has the Chinese gross at $2,155.69 million (identical to upper-bound figure). The Chinese gross cannot be any higher in dollars during the time that sum was grossed. It is only coming out higher now because the Chinese yuan has increased in value against the dollar.

We have a source that puts the non-Chinese gross at about $60 million. We have no reason to believe this is not accurate. :Wikipedia seems to be getting that figure from Box Office Mojo, but it's not correct. The figure in this article is sourced directly from the British Film Institute. According to the BFI, ''Paddington 2'' had grossed £42.7 million as [https://core-cms.bfi.org.uk/media/36378/download 3 November 2024], after 365 weeks of release. Depending on the exchange rate at the time, this would convert to $53–57 million.
:This is consistent with the $55.7 million that Box Office Mojo says it grossed on its [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl4068771585/weekend/ initial release]. There was a minor reissue in [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl4279336961/weekend/ October 2024]; according to BOM it grossed $42,398 in its first weekend and its overall total remained at around $55.7 million. It grossed $17,145 in its second weekend and then dropped off the chart. However, the $55.7 million that BOM recorded for that release was the total "to date" i.e. ''Paddington 2'' did not gross another $55 million in a reissue. BOM has just goofed by counting the running-total twice.
:The problem actually comes from the British Film Institute. They just treated the reissue as part of the initial release even though it was 7 years later, and updated the total. BOM has treated the updated lifetime total as the total for the reissue. But you can see even from the BOM it is wrong, because it opened with $42,398 and then somehow had $55.7 million after the weekend. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 18:45, 25 August 2026 (UTC)

:::::::The list is literally described in the following way: ''The following is a partial list of films that lost the most money, based on documented losses or estimated by expert analysis of various financial factors such as the production budget, marketing and distribution costs, '''gross box-office receipts and other ancillary revenues'''. The list is limited to films that are potentially among the highest box-office losses, adjusted for inflation (approximately upper-bound losses of $110 million or higher as of 2025).'' In modern-day accounting losses are calculated over a film's projected lifecycle and that is what is documented by this list. :::Mostly because it wasn't. Rynn Berry is not a credible authority on Hitler, and while Robert Payne actually met Hitler it was before the war. As explained in the article, all accounts of Hitler consuming meat pre-date his shift to vegetarianism. The last eyewitness account of Hitler consuming meat comes from 1937. Rynn Berry took these accounts out of context to prosecute his thesis that Hitler was never vegetarian. When his work was debunked, he conceded that Hitler may well have been vegetarian but not for "ethical reasons". That may or may not be true, but we will never know. Forensic analysis did not find any meat fibres in his teeth, and the woman who forced to become his food-taster in 1942 said that all of the food she was forced to test for Hitler was vegetarian. Hitler's vegetarianism did form part of Nazi propaganda, but for better or for worse all evidence points to the fact that he became vegetarian at the end of his life. * '''Comment''' I have reviewed the discussion and the diffs above. First of all, I believe the lead and the infobox are being conflated. Let's deal with the infobox first.
** The purpose of the "starring" field in the '''infobox''' is to identify the stars of the film. This should adhere to strict billing order. Usually the billing block identifies the billing order of the stars, but in this case the poster does not have one. Films often typically identify the stars in the film itself (either by listing them before the main title or after the main title with the word "starring"). I don't accept the main cast list at the end of the film is a valid mechanism for identifying the stars because this lists the entire cast and it does not clear make it explicitly clear who the stars are. An other solution is to defer to a reliable source, such as [https://variety.com/2025/film/reviews/dora-and-the-search-for-sol-dorado-review-dora-the-explorer-1236447571/ ''Variety''], who identify the principal cast as Samantha Lorraine, Jacob Rodriguez, Daniella Pineda, Gabriel Iglesias, Mariana Garzón Toro, and Acston Luca Porto. The order in the infobox should reflect the order in the source.
** As for the '''lead''' of the article, this is less formal and allows for a bit more discretion. It should list the stars of the film, but the lead can also identify other key members of the cast if the coverage in the article justifies mentioning them in the lead.
: The main thing here, is that you should use an objective criteria for determining the stars. The billing block on the poster is the usual way, but if not a available then either the opening credits of the film or a reliable source will suffice. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 23:36, 16 August 2025 (UTC)

items.post_text: :I think "animal horror" can come under "[[natural horror]]" or "[[creature feature]]", and obviously there is significant overlap between the two sub-genres. However, I would say there are instances where "animal horror" would not be counted as natural horror (instances where the story is more sci-fi based, for example), but it is difficult to envisage a scenario where an animal horror would not be counted as a creature feature. "Plant horror" is probably more aligned with "natural horror", but I think there may be outliers where plant horror could be perceived as sci-fi horror rather than natural horror. One example that springs to mind is ''The Day of the Triffids'' where the plants are alien in origin; ironically that is included on this list, but I can easily envisage a counter-argument where one would not consider it natural horror on the basis that the natural world is not the origin of the horror. * '''Oppose''' – The title is already sufficiently disambiguated. The nomination regurgitates earlier nominations (such as those at [[Talk:Star Wars (film)/Archive 8#Requested move 6 June 2016]] and [[Talk:Star Wars (film)/Archive 10#Requested move (January 2023)]]) and addresses none of the counter-arguments that successfully resisted the rename. A summary of the counter-arguments:
:# Most people are familiar with the name change history, but it's not relevant. No evidence has been presented that ''Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope'' is the [[WP:COMMONNAME]] (which would render this whole debate moot if that were the case)—the official name does not take automatic precedence per the rationale at [[WP:OFFICIALNAME]].
:# The nomination also advances the false notion that "A New Hope" would serve as necessary disambiguation. This is not so: the article is already sufficiently disambiguated through the '''(film)''' disambiguation term, in accordance with [[WP:NCFILMDAB]]. No evidence has been presented that ''Star Wars (film)'' is being confused with the franchise. WP:NCFILMDAB does not preclude natural disambiguation, but it does not mandate a preference either way.
:# One argument that I do have some sympathy for is the consistency argument per the 5th criterion at [[WP:CRITERIA]] (the title is consistent with the pattern of similar articles' titles). However, this has to be balanced against the 4th criterion of concision (the title is not longer than necessary to identify the article's subject and distinguish it from other subjects). In any case, the natural disambiguation argument would only stack up if ''[[The Empire Strikes Back]]'' and ''[[Return of the Jedi]]'' were to also undergo similar name changes; however, these two titles do not require disambiguation, so they would be moved away from their more concise common names purely for consistency reasons, effectively over-riding the most important naming convention ([[WP:COMMONNAME]]). In truth, I am on the fence when considering this article in isolation, but when taken with the two immediate sequels I cannot get on board with it, which means the consistency argument breaks down.

The fact that the film does not appear on lists of cult movies alongside firmly established cult movies is a real red-herring for me. Neither is the film being proclaimed a "cult" movie by writers recognized as experts in film analysis. There is also a slight concern in that all of the sources are Indian; ordinarily this would not be an issue from a factual perspective, but there are language differences between different varieties of English (even American English and British English) and we need to be sure that when these terms are used they are applied consistently. On the subject of consistency, we should probably ignore what is written at the film article itself, logical fallacy or not. If an article does not cover a film's purported "cult" status then I think that weakens the case for adding the film to the list,  but total consistency across all the articles would depend on all editors applying the same standards and that is difficult to achieve. We need to be pragmatic about it. This dispute brings to mind another article I regularly work on: the [[List of box-office bombs]]. Many films have been described as bombs that didn't actually bomb—they just slightly under-performed; we are lucky because we have been able to apply a financial criteria for inclusion. Unfortunately, a film's cult status cannot be objectively measured, but you can still bring a similar level of rigour to a film's subjective consideration by applying the principle at [[WP:BESTSOURCES]], coupled with WP:CONTEXTMATTERS. Applying those principles, I am not convinced by the available sources that ''Raaz'' is a suitable inclusion on this list. == Over-linking of names ==

An editor has taken to linking all of the names in the image captions, despite [[WP:REPEATLINK]] stating that terms should only be linked once, per major section. REPEATLINK permits repeat linking "'''if helpful'''". So far the editor in question has failed to explain why it is necessary to link the names yet again, when they are already linked multiple times in the table the images are situated next to. I accept there are instances where repeat linking is useful; for example, in sortable tables we cannot be sure in which order the names will occur. Similarly, it might be helpful to link the names in image captions if the images are not in close proximity to existing links, making it difficult to locate the link. This is not the case here. The editor's [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_highest-paid_film_actors&diff=prev&oldid=1330438074 reasoning] that the links are "literally harmless and is allowed by guideline" is not a valid rationale. We don't link terms because they are harmless, we only link terms if we can demonstrate that it would be helpful to do so. By linking the names in the captions, literally every occurrence of the name in the article is now linked. I fail to see how this is useful, or helpful. The onus is on editors adding links to demonstrate their utility. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 11:43, 31 December 2025 (UTC)

For example, is Nintendo just listed in there as a rights owner, or has it had a prominent role in producing and financing the film? Hard to say, really. Intuitively, I don't see why the nationality would be any different from the first film which is listed as co-production between United States and Japan, but we can't know for sure; by the same token I think we would need some compelling and explicit sourcing in order to deviate from that. * '''Comment''' Just to comment on the inconsistent approach of the BFI. I emailed them about this five years ago and, in short, it depends which ''department'' of the BFI is doing the classifying. The BFI Collections Database just uses the nationality of the production companies (which is why sometimes you will have several countries listed for a film); however, the Research and Statistic Unit attempts to take a more considered approach which takes into account a whole range of factors. Personally, I have found that the more discerning approach of the Research Unit tends to align better with the general perception of nationality identity (or "country of origin" as it is often known). The important thing to realize is that there is no universal approach and this is reflected in sources. The closest thing you will get to an "official" national identity is when a film is shot under an EU co-production treaty, but that doesn't really help us here. I believe that trying to determine the relative contributions of the various production companies is extremely challenging and probably comes under [[WP:OR]] anyway. The most relevant policy is [[WP:WEIGHT]] i.e. we should be looking to reflect how sources themselves categorise the film. This isn't straightforward either, given how few sources there are, and the inconsistency of the BFI on this matter (I would be much more willing to defer to the BFI if its two departments were aligned on the issue). The AFI Catalog has not logged it yet either, which further complicates the issue. However, I think it is rather telling that the Motion Pictures Producers of Japan (Eiren) do not consider it a Japanese move. On their [https://www.eiren.org/boxoffice_e/2023.html 2023 chart] they have it listed as the top "import", and omit it from their Japanese movies chart. If they had included it in the Japanese chart I would have been inclined to have listed Japan as a country of production, but if Japan itself does not claim it as one of their own films then it would seem rather contradictory for us to do so. On a final note, consensus can change as sources themselves are updated and as the film is added to various databases so one thing to bear in mind is that nothing is set in stone when it comes to these types of classifications, and it can be useful to review these things every few years. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 21:31, 5 February 2026 (UTC)

== Excessive number of images added to the article ==

It appears a dispute that originated at another article has spilled over into this article. It seems that {{u|Clarityfiend}} challenged {{u|Ariadne000}} about overly long image captions at [[The Day the Earth Stood Still]]. The discussion can be viewed at [[User_talk:Ariadne000#Film_captions]]. Clarityfiend provided several examples of articles which exhibited good practice, this article being one of those. Ariadne000 subsequently [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)&oldid=1291487093 added a dozen photos with overly long captions]. I find Ariadne000's general approach to editing problematic, but I will just focus on the editorial problems:
# I agree with Clarityfiend's view that overly long captions usually reflect poor practice per [[MOS:CAPSUCCINCT]]. In my experience, overly long captions are usually symptomatic of problems with the article body, or maybe the image's lack of relevance to the sourced commentary of the article.
# Ariadne000 argues that "because GWTW is so iconic, photos are warranted". There is no policy or guideline based rationale for such justification. There needs to be an encyclopedic purpose for including an image per [[MOS:IMAGERELEVANCE]]: "''Each image in an article should have a clear and unique illustrative purpose and serve as an important illustrative aid to understanding''". While a couple of the photos have encyclopedic value, in that they would useful to illustrate sourced commentary, the general deployment here is primarily decorative. 
# Just because the images are available and free doesn't mean we have to use them. There has been no regard for the aesthetic of the value, or how it may look on somebody else's screen (see the screencap here: https://postimg.cc/JG1MVWSY). A lot of care was taken in the positioning of images and files throughout the article e.g. the music file was placed in the music section, the reissue poster in the "Later releases" section, the premier photo in the "Premiere" section and so on. By jamming this many photos into the article, the original photos and files are no longer correctly aligned with the relevant section. To maintain this alignment across different resolutions, images were limited to one per section.

Ariadne000 is displaying a [[WP:BATTLEGROUND]] mentality and in [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)&diff=prev&oldid=1291483046 their edit summary] referred to me as a "bogus" account that "doesn't get an opinion". I have been around well over decade and took this article through its GA review. Every editor is entitled to an opinion, but I am the editor best placed to explain the original design decisions. I would urge them to make their case here for the encyclopedic value of the images they wish to add, and if there is a consensus to add them then we can look at integrating them into the article rather than simply dumping them and destroying the aesthetic of the article. # Re-structured version: [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Watership_Down_(film)&oldid=1300945994#BBFC_classification_revision_with_changing_attitudes_to_violence_in_children%E2%80%99s_films]

They take fundamentally different approaches. The original version introduces the controversy and then details the background over three subsequent paragraphs; namely: the BBFC, what initial critics thought, and recent criticism/scholarship. The new version approaches it in strictly chronologically fashion. I feel the first approach is more encyclopedic (and therefore more in keeping with Wikipedia) whereas the new version approaches it more as a news story with unfolding events.

I don't think the re-write is poor, but I do think it is inferior to the original version. I think the original version is far more succinct in summarizing the controversy, and then fleshing it out with background detail. I also find it mentally easier to parse (although I concede that may be because I am just more used to the original version). I would also like to add that I did not write the original version (so this is categorically not a case of me defending my own work). Generally, I don't think there are any policies/guidelines that would lead Wikipedia to prefer one over the other, so it is very much a personal preference thing. However, I would ask the anonymous editor to refrain from reverting and to respect [[WP:BRD]] until the issue is resolved. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 01:11, 18 July 2025 (UTC)

* '''Comment''' Before I tackle the substantive issue, I would like to point out that I have neither "stonewalled" the anonymous editor nor have I failed to enact [[Wikipedia:REVERT]] which actually advises to enact a partial revert, as opposed to a full revert, if there are some aspects of the edit that are acceptable. This can be confirmed by comparing the net effect of my partial revert: [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Watership_Down_%28film%29&diff=1300744482&oldid=1300479825]. I find it curious that the editor accuses me of stonewalling despite the fact that I have provided a full explanation for my revert here on the talk page, while the IP editor had to warned by an admin before engaging here.

:Just be clear: I do not think the IP's version is terrible, I just think it is inferior to what was already present in the article. I disagree that the section is about "the revision of the BBFC rating". The section is about the controversy that has resulted from changing attitudes about the film. The revised rating is only aspect of that. The questions that the IP poses are only relevant once you have articulated what the controversy is, otherwise the reader's typical response will be "Why are you telling me this?". You could make the case that the revised BBFC rating should be in the first paragraph too, but there is also an argument that by confining all of the BBFC stuff to the second paragraph helps to keep the section coherent. The section articulates the controversy in the first paragraph, and then brings in the relevant background over the successive three paragraphs addressing the rating revision, the initial critique, and modern reactions. It is well written, and the paragraphing—with each paragraph dealing with a separate aspect—gives the section a clean thematic structure. All of this is lacking in the re-write, as the editor simply "reports" the sequence of events. It makes it more difficult to parse, it's inherently less engaging and takes longer to get to the point.

:The irony here is that if I had written the section myself it probably would have been closer to the IP's version. I was active on the article when Cinefeline wrote the original section, and I think it is rather telling I didn't edit any part of it. Considering that the point of contention is the overall structure of the section I don't see much prospect of a compromise. If the IP is insists on installing their re-write, I suggest we drop a note at the relevant Wikiprojects and let the community decide, if the IP is agreeable to that? An editor has repeatedly removed the [http://www.screenonline.org.uk/people/id/453051/ Screenonline] link from the external links section, on the grounds it "gets her birthdate wrong" and that it "adds absolute nothing of worth". I don't agree that getting Christie's birthdate wrong bars the site from inclusion; for many years her dob was reported to be 1941 and many secondary sources still list it. Christie's entry also includes a comprehensive list of her credits up to 2005 (accessed from the righ-hand side of the page): http://www.screenonline.org.uk/people/id/453051/credits.html; broadcast dates are also included with her TV appearances. In this respect it is more comprehensive than IMDB which the editor apparently does not have an issue with. Furthermore, the page also includes an index of pages related to key credits in her filmography, which in turn include materials such as stills, posters, clips and information about the films themselves. Taken collectively, I believe the page meets the criteria offered at [[WP:ELYES]] and IMO offers more information value than Christie's IMDb page which is a mainstay on actor biographies. items.post_text: ::::::::I have also reverted the key to the previous version. The whole concept of the ratings system is the notion of unrestricted, restricted and prohibitive categories, and the highlighting in the chart is tied to that distinction. To take the United States as an example, a PG-13 is advisory: it is not recommended for children below that age but it is not restricted, either. The "R" rating applies a mandatory parental restriction whereas NC-17 is prohibitive. These latter two ratings are not advisory. If they were, then they would be shaded purple. items.post_text: ::::::::::I suppose the real question here, does removing explicit language actually make it clearer? Not everyone evaluates language in the same way: for example, if English is a second-language or if you are autistic. Being clear about whether a rating is unrestricted, restricted or prohibitive removes any ambiguity that could be read into the interpretation. The worst case scenario by explicitly stating if a classification category is restrictive or not is that it does not make it any clearer; the worst case scenario in not explicitly stating it is that it may become ambiguous for some people. It's not clear to me why you think removing explicit labels improves the article. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 09:48, 23 February 2026 (UTC)
items.discussion_title: Fiji has reintroduced the PG rating

items.post_text: ::::::::::::This is not the same as explicitly saying whether a classification is advisory/restricted/prohibitive etc. Saying somebody "must not" do something can still be interpreted as strong advice, as opposed to a mandatory requirement. Different cultures have different language formalisms. Autistic people also process language differently. It is only when you make it clear that a rating is restricted/prohibitive that all ambiguity is removed. Some classification bodies also make this distinction, such as the [https://www.classification.gov.au/classification-ratings/what-are-ratings Australian Classification Board]. I have no problem with you adding further text to add further clarification to the key, but removing descriptors that clarify whether a rating is advisory/restrictive/prohibitive does not add clarity, it creates potential ambiguity. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 03:38, 24 February 2026 (UTC)

== Addition of images to the article ==
An editor has repeatedly added multiple images to the article, per [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)&diff=prev&oldid=1384132145], [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)&diff=prev&oldid=1384132145] and [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gone_with_the_Wind_(film)&diff=prev&oldid=1384211756]. I have repeatedly asked them to follow [[WP:BRD]] and initiate a discussion on the article talk page; I had hoped the editor would have adhered to thus guidance but apparently not, so I have taken the liberty of initiating the discussion instead.

;Inclusion
The editor's rationale appears to be that many articles about classic films have "loads of photos". This may be true, but this is a byproduct of the images themselves being in the public domain, not the product of a encyclopedic based rationale. The reasons the editor advanced on my talk page are
# illustrate the cast
# illustrate the production style
# give a graphic representation of the plot summary
# add visual interest to the article

These are not valid reasons in themselves. The relevant guideline for image inclusion is [[MOS:IMAGEREL]]. The pertinent bit states {{quote|''Images must be significant and relevant in the topic's context, not primarily decorative. Each image in an article should have a clear and unique illustrative purpose and serve as an important illustrative aid to understanding the subject ... However, not every article needs images, and too many can be distracting or cause undue weight: usually, less is more.''}}

* In this context the editors fourth reason is simply not valid per [[WP:NOTGALLERY]] (i.e. we don't add images to an article simply for the sake of adding images to the article). 
* The third reason is also a stretch: plot summaries do not need a "graphic representation". Wikipedia is not a comic-book. Plot summaries are descriptive by nature; indeed, both the American Film Catalog and IMDb get by without incorporating images of the plot. I cannot think of a single film article on Wikipedia where it has been necessary to add an image to the plot to help a reader further their understanding of the plot.
* The first reason is the most valid; however we don't "illustrate" the cast we "identify" the cast. It is worth bearing in mind that in this capacity a cast member usually only needs to be visually identified once, although if they further appear in "group" photos this is acceptable. The editor added an image of Leslie Howard and Olivia de Havilland to the cast section; I am actually open to this, as I agree that it would be a useful addition to the article, but there needs to be regard to the placement.
* The second reason is also valid to the extent that the production style needs to be illustrated i.e. whatever they are illustrating should be the subject of commentary. [[WP:NOTGALLERY]] clarifies this: "If you are interested in presenting a picture, please provide an encyclopedic context". In this context, I think the still of the Tara plantation meets the relevant criteria. The addition of the wedding costumes to the costumes section is primarily decorative. Yes, it's a costume, but it does not illustrate the concepts that are discussed. Furthermore, the section is too small to fully accommodate an image.

;Placement
The final point regards the concept of image placement, which the editor seems to have trouble with. The first couple of edits we just got an image dump. In the third we got a bit more effort, but it is worth bearing in mind what [[WP:GALLERY]] states: {{quote|''In articles that have several images, they are typically placed individually near the relevant text ... Generally, a gallery or cluster of images should not be added so long as there is space for images to be effectively presented adjacent to text.''}}

I have two points to make in this regard:
* The image should be in close proximity to the text that gives it encyclopedic value. If the image comes too early, the reader will not appreciate its significance; too late, and the reader has moved on. Ideally the text and the image should be in the same frame. Image dumps rarely achieve this because the images come first push the later images down, so they are no longer adjacent to the text. This defeats the purpose of adding the images in the first place. Given that displays are of different sizes, adding more than one image to a sub-section generally creates problems. If you intend to add more than one image, you should check how the article renders at ~1,000 pixels and at ~2,000 pixels wide, to ensure that the structure of the article remains robust. 
* When you add an image to a short-sub-section, or more than one image to a longer section the images can often protrude into the next section. Not only does this have ramifications for image placement in the next section, it is aesthetically poor and makes the article look amateurish. This is the primary problem with adding the image of Howard and de Havilland to the casting section—on wider displays it protrudes into the next section.

;Conclusion
So far, the editor's edits have been disruptive in that the addition of images has not been in accordance with the relevant style guidelines, and their manner has been combative rather than collegiate. I ask them to not add the images back into the article until the issues have been resolved and they have obtained a consensus for them. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 08:35, 8 November 2026 (UTC)

The article remained in that form for over 13 years, until a couple of months ago when {{u|TheVictoriaHarbourer}} overhauled the article. The triple crown article already provides the proper version of this table, so it does not need to be included in an article detailing the corporate structure of the tour i.e. tournament results do not come under the scope of the article. I have removed it for now per [[WP:STATUSQUO]]. If TheVictoriaHarbourer strongly feels the table should be included then he should advance a case for it and obtain a consensus. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 14:09, 26 April 2025 (UTC)

items.post_text:
* '''Option 3''' – both dates with an accompanying note. Wikipedia has a preference for secondary sources over primary sources and the 1988 date dominates in that respect. A strict interpretation of [[WP:BLPPRIMARY]] and [[WP:WEIGHT]] would favor the 1988 date. However, there are numerous secondary sources that give an age that is consistent with 1987, rather than 1988, as per [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vanessa_Kirby&oldid=1310132902#cite_note-born-7 the note in the article]. The [https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/drama/who-is-vanessa-kirby-from-the-crown/ Radio Times] also gives 1987 as the year of her birth. It should also be noted that [https://www.imdb.com/name/nm3948952/ IMDB] goes with the 1987 date; while not a reliable source, IMDB is fairly accurate on the whole when it comes to birth dates. The most compelling evidence comes from primary sources, though:
** Public records for England and Wales show that there was no Vanessa Kirby born in 1988; and only one was [https://postimg.cc/gallery/gRD5Wzm born in 1987]. As you can see from the birth record the mother of the one born in 1987 has the same maiden name as the actress.
** The actress also has her own production company, [https://variety.com/2024/film/global/vanessa-kirby-aluna-labs-emerging-female-filmmakers-1236027204/ Aluna Entertainment]. The [https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/officers/nb0A4AKLrxOmZBmyJc2Tciz_Pf4/appointments government registration for this company] has Kirby's date of birth logged as April 1987. It should be noted that it is a criminal offence to provide false details to Companies House, and you also have to provide identification too.
:IMO, the primary sources (especially the government registration of her company} makes a compelling case for the 1987 date. While I appreciate that BLPPRIMARY establishes an important principle—it essentially exists to prevent editors creating "new" information that does not exist in secondary sources—I believe that strict observance in this case put Wikipedia in a position of propagating misinformation. The primary goal of Wikipedia is to disseminate facts. We do not actually need the primary sources to source the 1987 date so we would not actually be using primary sources to create new information, but just to reinforce the notion that there is factual discrepancy. We don't have to pick a side in these types of debates: presenting the case for both is a strength of Wikipedia. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 22:58, 7 September 2025 (UTC)

Secondary sources already exist to support the 1987 date, albeit they are in the minority. What some of us are saying is that public records in this case strongly suggest the 1988 date is incorrect. If the dob on the company registration is wrong, then either Kirby or her legal representatives must have provided the incorrect dob, and Companies House must have overlooked that it did not match her identification documents. Personally, I don't think it is very likely that Kirby submitted the 1987 date in error, although I accept it is possible. This is compounded by the fact that birth record transcripts also show there were no Vanessa Kirbys born in 1988, but there was one born in 1987 to a woman with the maiden name "Cooper". I see you have a BSc and MSc; therefore you have been formally trained to assess to what extent the available evidence supports a theory. Putting aside Wikipedia's various policies and guidelines for the moment, are you saying that in your considered judgment these public records do not give you pause for thought that the 1988 date is incorrect? I don't see why IAR does not apply to this case; in fact I think situations like these are what IAR is designed for. I don't believe the intention of BLPPRIMARY is to encourage us to disseminate misinformation, or at least information we have compelling reasons to suspect is wrong, on the basis that it solely enjoys more support from secondary sources. Back-to-back wins do not define an era: if the Chinese dominate the next decade, then the labeling the IP editor is attempting to install would be more meritorious, but there are multiple stories going on here: not so much Chinese emergence, but Chinese breakthrough; but also the ongoing internationalization of the game at the top level, and the fact that we've had four consecutive new champions when we only had five in the first two decades of the 21st century. * '''Comment''' I oppose re-framing the definition as ethical opposition to speciesism. Definitions of veganism do not generally invoke speciesism—they are generally grounded in rejecting the exploitation of animals; speciesism is concerned with animal exploitation too, but it's a philosophy that draws parallels between the agency of other species and that of people. This article covers the different aspects of veganism—ranging from ethical veganism to environmental veganism to religious or cultural veganism. We shouldn't be prioritising one particular form of veganism over another in the lead—this comes off as advocacy rather than encyclopedic commentary. The [https://www.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/definition/english/veganism dictionary] provides a basic definition based around eating and using animal products, and the [https://www.vegansociety.com/go-vegan/definition-veganism Vegan Society] fleshes this out a bit. The definition in the lead doesn't need to be any more complicated than that. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 04:07, 26 May 2026 (UTC)

:*:I don't think veganism necessarily precludes visiting a zoo, in the same it doesn't necessarily rule out buying a veggie burger from MacDonalds, although many vegans definitely rule those things out. As this [https://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/45274517 BBC article] says, a vegan  is "someone who doesn't eat or use animal products". The pure definition verifiably extends beyond just a diet, but the diet is generally the only thing that all vegans agree on. An environmental vegan is sometimes ok with buying second-hand leather products because it doesn't directly contribute to animal exploitation and contributes to sustainability, but an ethical vegan would not because an animal still died to create the product. Vegans often make exceptions for medication (which has often been tested on animals or may even use an animal derivative), which would actually be precluded from the pure definition. I work a lot on the [[List of vegans]], and the sources overwhelmingly only discuss diet, so it's not clear how "vegan" somebody is in other aspects of their life. So I think veganism extends beyond a diet, but there is not a strict consensus about what that entails. Usually, when someone is a dietary vegan and that choice carries over to no other aspect of their life (maybe it's a health kick or something) they are said to practice a plan-based diet. In practice, being a vegan generally involves not consuming animal derivatives as part of a diet and adopting a lifestyle that is less dependent on animal exploitation in other areas. In my experience, someone who does that would usually be regarded as a vegan or practicing veganism. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 16:21, 26 May 2026 (UTC)

items.post_text: == Use of "frac" vs. Unicode ½ vs HTML entity ½ == Hi folks, I'm sure there's a good reason for this, but why is Fellini's movie 8½ described using 'frac' i.e. with {{frac|8|1|2}} ({{frac|8|1|2}})? This seems to offer little improvement over the actual Unicode 'half' character ('½') which is used in the wikilink anyway. If a user's system doesn't support ½, then it won't be able to open the link to that article – though I suppose in that edge case, you could argue that at least this article might display OK even if the link doesn't work. If Unicode is a stretch, how about an HTML entity? They've been a W3C recommendation since 1999, so unlikely to cause even the oldest of web-capable devices to break a sweat. That would make the film's title 8½ in the source, which is pretty human-readable if you can't have "8½". I wouldn't have noticed if 'frac' worked. But on my Mac (running Firefox on Mac OS 11 Big Sur) the text appeared initially as "8 1/2", then after I looked at the source and subsequently cancelled, it started appering as "8+1/2"! Looks like an issue with Template:Fraction, the Mediawiki codebase, or perhaps something else. The source for Template:Fraction appears to be here. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Fraction/styles.css == Semi-protected edit request on 30 May 2026 == {{Resolved|Entry has been deleted [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 21:45, 30 May 2026 (UTC)

* You are on very thin ice now. Just to cover the basics:
# Do NOT trivia such as when filming started on a film, such as [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1970_in_film&diff=prev&oldid=1366343806 did at 1970 in film]. The date a film started filming—even one as significant as ''The Godfather'' is not inherently a significant event in itself, unless there was something significant about the start of filming. Followjng your logic, we could add the end-of-filming date too, and not just for ''The Godfather'' but also for many other films. And how would we determine which films to do this for. This is [[WP:INDISCRIMINATE]] information and does not belong on Wikipedia. The same goes for anniversaries of various films too.
# If something significant happens in a later year, then it should be documented in the article about that year. [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2019_in_film&diff=1366344996&oldid=1366252781 Edits such as these] are not relevant. The fact that a record is overtaken at a later date is a significant fact about the film (that should go in the film article) and a significant fact that occurs in the later year (which should be documented at the appropriate article). It is not a significant fact about 2019 (as in the example here) so does not belong in this article. Put information where it is relevant.
# [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2023_in_film&diff=prev&oldid=1366346964 Here is an example] of something that is both [[WP:UNDUE]] and unsourced. All remaining films released in 1927 still under copyright in the United States entered the public domain in 2023. So did ''The Jazz Singer''. We do not need to single out one particular film. The other issue is that claims about films entering the public domain are a non-trivial factual claim and, as such, need to be sourced. [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2013_in_film&diff=1366347651&oldid=1366254523 Adding a "citation needed" tag] does not mitigate the need to add a source. Nobody should be adding content and the tag at the same time. If you can source it then source it, but if you can't then don't add it!
# Sources should corroborate the claim they accompany, but that is not the case [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1994_in_film&diff=1366343356&oldid=1366242902 in this example]. Neither source makes the claim about either film that they are consistently rated the greatest ever. You may be able to locate a source that makes the claim that these films are among the greatest ever (which these sources do not do), but if you are going to make the claim that they are '''consistently''' rated as the greatest, then you need a source to that effect. Even then, I question whether a qualitative assessment from many years later because in an article about events that occurred in 1994. That aside, I reverted your edit on the grounds that the sources did not back up the central claim.

If you are unsure about something then ask on the talk page. :There were some bits that were ok but, as I alluded to in my edit summary, I considered it inferior to the existing version. :::::Not really. Cyan is not superior to gray because cyan’s identity depends heavily on blue and green perception. It can be difficult to distinguish it from green in the case of Tritanopia, and difficult to distinguish from blue in the case of deuteranopia. White, gray and black are your core colors. After that, I would say blue & yellow because protanopia/deuteranopia (red/green deficiencies) is far more common than tritanopia (blue/yellow color blindness). But this is getting off the subject now; I reverted you because your provided no rationale for restructuring the table, and when I pushed you on your reason I did not get a coherent scientific reason. :::I don't understand what a "visual design improvement" means in this context. In the version on the left, the top row houses all of the psychological primary colors starting with yellow & blue, which are less common in color blindness (red/green blindness is more common). While editors are free to choose from any column, it makes sense to use the ordering of the colors to encourage colors that are less common in color blindness. You also have the anochromatic (white/black shades of gray) on the top row too; in reality, if you only need 2–3 colours it would actually be better to use the anochromatic spectrum. Ultimately the table appears to be designed from an accessibility perspective, not a visual design one. It's best not to alter things if you don't understand the reasons why it was designed that way in the first place. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan#top|talk]]) 15:39, 21 May 2026 (UTC)

::Why are you so invested in making the table sortable? Generally, tables are only made sortable on Wikipedia if there are valid encyclopedic reasons for doing so. There are no encyclopedic reasons in this case, because it is a chronology. Sorting on the title doesn't serve any purpose, while sorting on the gross and the budget is meaningless because some cells hold more than one amount. The only reason you have provided for sorting the table is to reduce the amount of scrolling that is needed to reach the more recent years; on the other hand, we don't generally make row-spanned columns sortable because the sort function loses the integrity of the row-spanning. In any case, javascript does not work for everyone, so even if the table were made to be sortable it would not benefit every reader. If you think the way the table is organised is sub-optimal i.e. it would be better have the more recent years at the top, then it would make more sense to re-organise the table to that effect. ::::The other claims you cite are not unsourced, and they are different in nature. It is just a point of fact that Jaws is the prototypical summer blockbuster, and that aspect is covered in substantial detail throughout the article, and attributed to many sources. How "great" something is is a subjective opinion, not a fact. Firstly, a subjective opinion should not be offered in Wikipedia's voice, it should be attributed. Secondly, just because we can source a few lists of great films in which ''Jaws'' appears does not inherently make it one of the greatest films of all-time, in just the same way a bunch of positive reviews doesn't necessarily make a film well reviewed. We can say the claim has been made by this person or that list (which is what the article does) but we should refrain from drawing our own conclusions. Thirdly, proclaiming something the "greatest" (or one of) is an exceptional claim, which should require [[WP:EXCEPTIONAL]] sources, which simply do not exist in the article for this specific claim. kind.description: They discuss film earnings, budgets, losses, and financial rankings. They identify double-counted re-release earnings and argue that loss estimates must include income beyond cinemas. They compare box-office databases, archived figures, studio corrections, and industry reporting, using Wikipedia’s sourcing rules and consistent list criteria to decide which figures to include and when updates are justified.

examples.post_text:
== Box Office Mojo vs The Numbers ==

You will find that that BOM and The Numbers very rarely have the same figure for any film and, as such, which we have to make a decision about which figure to use. Obviously—this being a chart—you have to pick one. The BOM double-counting issue aside, we have found that BOM is generally better overall for accuracy than The Numbers, so there has been a long-standing tradition to default to BOM in the article—especially for the main chart—unless there is clear evidence that the figure is incorrect and another source offers a more accurate number. Sometimes the numbers fall out of sync because one source is updated before the other, but this in itself is not a good reason for defaulting to a different source, because Wikipedia is [[WP:NOTNEWS]]. If we know the source will be updated in the near future we can stick with the current source and wait for it to be updated. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 22:46, 17 February 2026 (UTC)
examples.discussion_title: Box Office Mojo vs The Numbers

examples.post_text: :They employ different methodologies., so are representing different types of losses. This article assesses overall loss (including projected ancillary revenue). This is what [https://deadline.com/2025/03/snow-white-bombs-rachel-zegler-1236354912/ Deadline] states: {{quote|Disney‘s Rachel Zegler– and Gal Gadot-starring Snow White is headed to an estimated loss of $115 million after all global home entertainment, TV and Disney+ ancillaries, according to distribution sources Monday. The loss, which was expected, is based on a final worldwide box office of $225M.}} [https://www.forbes.com/sites/carolinereid/2026/02/10/disney-loses-170-million-on-snow-white-as-studio-reveals-movie-blew-its-budget/ Forbes] makes it clear the $170 million loss is based only on the box-office take: {{quote|The share of the box office isn’t the studio’s only return from a movie so offsetting it from the costs in the financial statements does not show whether it made a profit or a loss overall. As a Disney spokesperson told me in 2023, "there will be other income generated by the production (such as DVD/Blu Ray sales, merchandising, etc.). It’s not reflecting a true account of whether the film was overall profitable."}} So the two publications are using different methodologies to assess the level of failure. The Deadline approach is the one that is more consistent with the other entries on the list; it's true it's an early estimate, but Deadline will probably review the calculation when it does its round-up of 2025 flops, and The Numbers may revise that further. While Forbes is the most accurate source for budgets (because it accesses audited accounts through HMRC) its loss calculations are just estimates, that ignore several important factors. [[User:Betty Logan|Betty Logan]] ([[User talk:Betty Logan|talk]]) 00:54, 2 March 2026 (UTC)

:The update is almost certainly an issue with BOM: [[Wikipedia:WikiProject_Film/Film_finance_task_force#Box_Office_Mojo]]. The overseas gross was originally recorded as $450.6 million, and then at some point in 2024 it was randomly updated to $458.2 million. Whilst it is not impossible it could be a correction, an erroneous change to an initial gross figure in the case of films that have had re-releases is a long-standing issue with BOM. Sometimes the local distributor submits the full lifetime gross, which—depending on how they report it—leads to double-counting as part of the original gross or as part of the re-release gross. In the case of ''The Lion King'', this is almost certainly what happened, because [https://www.boxofficemojo.com/article/ed3093300228/ Disney itself issued a correction] to Box Office Mojo in 2016 where they clarified that ''The Lion King'' had indeed grossed $450.6 million overseas on its original release. Is it possible that Disney have corrected the gross yet again? It's not impossible, but there has been no reporting to that effect and given the known double-counting issue with BOM I would say it is strong odds the new figure is incorrect. kind.description: They argue that calling Jaws one of the greatest films is subjective and should be attributed, not stated as fact. They cite Wikipedia rules against drawing independent conclusions and requiring strong evidence for exceptional claims. They distinguish this claim from its status as a pioneering summer blockbuster, which the article supports with many sources.

examples.post_text: ::::The other claims you cite are not unsourced, and they are different in nature. It is just a point of fact that Jaws is the prototypical summer blockbuster, and that aspect is covered in substantial detail throughout the article, and attributed to many sources. How "great" something is is a subjective opinion, not a fact. Firstly, a subjective opinion should not be offered in Wikipedia's voice, it should be attributed. Secondly, just because we can source a few lists of great films in which ''Jaws'' appears does not inherently make it one of the greatest films of all-time, in just the same way a bunch of positive reviews doesn't necessarily make a film well reviewed. We can say the claim has been made by this person or that list (which is what the article does) but we should refrain from drawing our own conclusions. Thirdly, proclaiming something the "greatest" (or one of) is an exceptional claim, which should require [[WP:EXCEPTIONAL]] sources, which simply do not exist in the article for this specific claim.
